Omissions

1. No documented quality-assurance and calibration regime for playback accuracy and fidelity across all line types and host sites.

The plan targets >95% successful digitization and >80% reconstruction accuracy but does not specify how these metrics are measured, calibrated or validated consistently across 30+ units and three line types (Tape, Film, Card). No reference media set, inter-unit drift detection or archival-standard playback verification is mentioned. This is critical because success claims rest on evidence the plan does not yet collect, and archivists will demand proof before releasing unique materials.

Recommendation: By Month 4 (2027-02-12), establish a Reference Media Calibration Set: procure 10–15 standard-condition tape reels, film cans and card batches from known sources. At each new unit deployment, digitize the reference set and measure against baseline (azimuth, speed regulation, signal-to-noise ratio, colour accuracy). Publish a Playback Fidelity Dashboard showing all units' performance against reference standards. If any unit drifts >5% from baseline, trigger re-calibration or removal. Budget USD 500K–1M for reference-media procurement and quarterly inter-unit calibration.

2. No explicit data-custody and perpetual-storage plan beyond Month 120 (2036-10-12), creating an orphaned 200+ PB archive with no steward.

The plan targets 200+ PB recovered but does not specify who holds the masters, in what formats, with how many verified copies, or how costs are funded after the 10-year programme closes. Without a clear end-state, the recovered data itself becomes a liability: no institution may accept perpetual storage obligations, format-migration costs are not budgeted, and the archive may be inaccessible or degraded within 5–10 years of Month 120 (2036-10-12). This undermines the entire preservation mission.

Recommendation: By Month 12 (2027-10-12), establish a Custody and Perpetual Storage Working Group tasked with deciding: (a) where masters live (host-held vs. federated network vs. central); (b) format standards (preservation master format, access derivative formats, migration triggers); (c) number of verified copies and geographic separation; (d) funding model post-Month 120 (2036-10-12) (endowment, cost-sharing with archives, government commitment). By Month 36 (2029-10-12), publish a Custody and Access Plan binding partner archives to multi-decade storage commitments. Budget USD 2M–5M from Phase 3 for data-migration and storage-sustainability planning.

3. No defined role for independent third-party audit and verification of recovery claims, recovery rates and success metrics.

The plan's headline targets (3.6M items, 200+ PB, >95% success, >80% accuracy) are stated but not independently validated. Self-reporting by the programme team invites optimistic metrics; funders and partner archives have no credible evidence that these targets are being met. Gate releases hinge on unverified success metrics, risking a Phase 2 decision based on inflated pilot results.

Recommendation: By Month 3 (2027-01-12), establish an Independent Verification and Audit Regime: contract an external auditor (third-party preservation lab or consultancy) to sample recovered items at each site, compare against originals, and publish precision, recall and quality metrics per format and degradation level. Conduct quarterly audits (sampling 2–5% of recovered content per site). Publish results monthly in a public Verification Dashboard. Gate releases depend on third-party findings, not internal reports. Budget USD 1M–2M for independent audits over the programme.

4. Absence of a defined incident-response and near-miss reporting system across the fleet, creating blind spots on equipment failures, handling damage and close calls.

The plan mentions incident protocols but does not specify who logs failures, how data is aggregated, who analyzes patterns or how systematic issues (e.g. all Film Line units showing humidity-control drift) are escalated. Without central incident tracking, failure modes go undetected, root-cause analysis is impossible, and the same failure repeats across multiple units before remediation.

Recommendation: By Month 6 (2027-04-12), establish a Centralized Incident and Failure Tracking System: every unit crew logs equipment failures, handling anomalies and near-misses within 4 hours via a secure web portal (equipment-ID, symptom, action taken, outcome). Automated daily aggregate to Central Operations and Fleet Management Officer. Weekly pattern detection: flag if any failure signature (e.g. 'tape transport azimuth drift') appears >1 time in a week across the fleet. Monthly root-cause analysis (engineering team + retired-mentor review). Quarterly trend reports to Programme Board. Budget USD 300K–500K for incident-tracking software and 1 FTE incident analyst.

5. No role or team dedicated to managing the knowledge base and digital scholarship access post-Month 120 (2036-10-12).

The plan states that recovered data has 'post-human value' and should be accessible to future AI and researchers, but no team owns the knowledge commons, documentation or digital-scholarship platform beyond the 10-year programme. Without a steward, the knowledge base (mentoring curricula, vintage-equipment specs, repair procedures, AI model versions) may become inaccessible or lost after Month 120 (2036-10-12).

Recommendation: By Month 24 (2028-10-12), establish a Digital Knowledge Commons working group to design a public-facing platform (wiki, repository, or open-access archive) for knowledge artifacts: mentoring curricula, vintage-equipment technical specs, repair procedures, AI model versions and provenance, quality-control workflows. By Month 36 (2029-10-12), deploy the platform. By Month 90 (2034-04-12), ensure platform governance and stewardship are handed to a successor institution (university, national library or non-profit heritage body). Budget USD 1M–2M for platform development and 1 FTE knowledge manager throughout the programme.

6. No explicit environmental sustainability or end-of-life recycling plan for 30 containers, 300–500 vintage machines and consumables at programme closure.

The plan does not address what happens to the containerized units, vintage equipment, and hazardous consumables (baking-oven internals, solvents, electronics) after Month 120 (2036-10-12). Without a documented end-of-life plan, these assets may be landfilled (environmental violation), stored indefinitely (cost burden), or transferred without proper documentation (liability exposure).

Recommendation: By Month 12 (2027-10-12), develop an Equipment Sunset and Recycling Plan specifying: (a) which units are retained for ongoing deployment (if any); (b) which are transferred to universities or archives with maintenance commitments; (c) which are decommissioned, with certified e-waste recycling and hazmat disposal protocols; (d) which vintage machines are donated to makers-spaces or museums (with condition assessment and liability waivers). By Month 60 (2031-10-12), identify receiving institutions and obtain written commitments. Budget USD 500K–1.5M for decommissioning, recycling and responsible equipment transfer.

Potential Improvements

1. Clarify and reconcile the staffing model and operating-expense budget at Phase 1 scale before pilot design freezes.

The plan allocates 50–60 staff per active MIU and USD 2–3M annual opex per unit. Recomputation suggests payroll alone at USD 50–70K per staff member equals USD 2.5–4.2M per unit-year, leaving USD 0–0.7M for all other costs (equipment, parts, logistics, utilities). At face value, either staffing or budget assumptions are unfeasible. Without clarity by Month 4 (2027-02-12), Phase 2 commitments rest on a cost model that will fail.

Recommendation: By Month 1 (2026-11-12), commission an independent operational cost audit of one active broadcast or archive digitization operation (e.g. Indiana University MDPI, Library of Congress Packard Campus) to benchmark salaries, loaded costs and opex per unit-year in comparable settings. By Month 2 (2026-12-12), restate the CDDIN budget with itemized line-item detail: salaries (by role), benefits and taxes, travel and visa, equipment and parts, consumables, utilities, satellite/fiber, insurance, overhead. Model three staffing scenarios (50–60, 35–40, 20–25 per unit) and show cost per scenario. By Month 4 (2027-02-12), lock the staffing and budget model; if reconciliation requires <25 staff per unit, adjust Months 24–120 (2028-10-12 to 2036-10-12) headcount planning accordingly or increase the budget cap.

2. Establish explicit success gates and decision criteria before Phase 1 operations begin, reducing ambiguity in gate releases.

The plan lists success metrics (>95% digitization, >80% accuracy, <20% review, >90% uptime) but does not define what 'sustained' means (3 months? 6 months?), how many sites must achieve it (2? 3?), or what constitutes a gate-release decision vs. a rework scenario. Ambiguous gates delay Phase 2 release and create funder disputes.

Recommendation: By Month 1 (2026-11-12), convene the Programme Board and publish a Phase 1 Gate Release Charter specifying: (a) metrics (>95% digitization success = zero unrecoverable items in a batch of 1,000+; >80% reconstruction accuracy = third-party sampling comparison; <20% review = actual flagging rate measured over 3+ months; >90% uptime = trailing 6-month measurement); (b) duration (all metrics held for ≥3 consecutive months); (c) sites (≥2 different archives); (d) variance tolerance (±5% acceptable, >10% triggers rework assessment); (e) override rule (best-efforts at ≥80% of targets allows conditional tranche, not full release). Obtain written board approval and publish publicly by Month 3 (2027-01-12).

3. Create a dedicated Funder Engagement and Commitment Registry to track pledge-to-commitment conversion and identify funding gaps early.

The plan lists 15+ funders (government, philanthropic, technology sector) with pledged amounts but no registry tracking which pledges are binding committed contracts vs. best-effort statements. Without visibility into commitment status, programme leadership cannot assess cash flow risk or identify contingency sources early enough to avoid gate delays.

Recommendation: By Month 1 (2026-11-12), establish a Funding Commitment Registry with entries for each funder: organization name, pledged amount, commitment status (pledged, intent-to-commit, committed with conditions, fully committed), expected release schedule (annual tranches?), contingency conditions (gates, milestones, variance limits). By Month 2 (2026-12-12), conduct outreach to each funder to convert pledges into binding contracts by Month 3 (2027-01-12). Target ≥50% (USD 30M) of Phase 1 committed. For unresolved pledges, identify 2–3 backup funders or a USD 15–20M bridge-credit line. Update registry monthly.

4. Define and document the Remote Diagnostics and Expert Routing system architecture before central operations begins.

The plan mentions remote expert guidance and central operations but does not specify how a field crew accesses a retired-engineer mentor for a tape-deck azimuth problem, how priority is assigned (which expert? how fast?), or what happens if the mentor is unavailable. Ad-hoc expert routing will delay repairs and create uptime variance.

Recommendation: By Month 3 (2027-01-12), design the Remote Diagnostics architecture: (a) field crew logs a failure (equipment type, symptom, troubleshooting steps taken) via a mobile app or secure web form with photos; (b) automated triage routes to the appropriate specialist (retired-engineer mentor for legacy deck, parts engineer for fabrication, AI specialist for signal issues); (c) specialist responds within 4 hours with phone/video guidance or a parts recommendation; (d) escalation after 24 hours to Central Operations and Fleet Management Officer if unresolved. Build a simple ticketing system (open-source or cloud-based) and test with the first pilot. Budget USD 200K–300K for remote-diagnostics software and training.

5. Introduce a formal change-control and design-review process for containerized unit architecture before Phase 2 procurement.

The plan does not specify how design changes (e.g. upgraded climate control, reinforced robotic arm) are reviewed, tested and approved before being replicated into 12 Phase 2 units. Without formal design governance, unproven changes risk cascading rework across the fleet at cost and schedule penalty.

Recommendation: By Month 4 (2027-02-12), establish a Design Review Gate (DRG) process: every material change to the MIU (container retrofit, equipment selection, software upgrade, control logic) must be reviewed by an independent panel (2–3 subject-matter experts from the mentor pool and engineering team) before design freeze. Changes are approved, rejected, or requested for testing. Design freeze for Phase 2 units occurs by Month 20 (2028-06-12), allowing 4 months for long-lead procurement. Changes identified after freeze are documented as 'Phase 2.1' rework and flagged for Phase 3 incorporation, not mid-Phase 2 retrofit. Publish change log monthly.

6. Establish a working group to define and enforce data-format standards for preservation masters and derivatives across all units.

The plan does not specify what preservation master formats are required (raw wideband for tape? lossless codec?), what access derivatives are created (MP3? JPEG2000?), or how formats are versioned and migrated over decades. Inconsistent formats across 30 units create archive integration headaches and risk format-obsolescence lock-in.

Recommendation: By Month 6 (2027-04-12), establish a Data Format Standards Working Group (archivists, signal-processing engineers, preservation community liaisons) to publish preservation-format specifications for each line type (Tape, Film, Card). Specify master format (e.g. FLAC or uncompressed WAV for audio, TIFF or DPX for film, text or PDF for cards), metadata schema (Dublin Core or equivalent), access-derivative formats and transcoding rules. Test formats on all 3 pilot units. By Month 12 (2027-10-12), publish the standard and enforce it fleet-wide. Reserve USD 500K for format research and validation.

7. Create a Site Readiness Scorecard and Pre-Deployment Checklist to reduce ad-hoc delays and ensure consistent site preparation.

The plan mentions site readiness but does not specify what 'ready' means: power capacity, hardstand condition, fire-authority approval, insurer letter, staff liaison, security access? Without a standard scorecard, deployments are delayed by missing preconditions that could have been identified months in advance.

Recommendation: By Month 2 (2026-12-12), develop a Site Readiness Scorecard with mandatory criteria: (a) power (208–240V, ≥200 kW stable or generator backup); (b) hardstand (level concrete, ≥50m × 15m); (c) security (perimeter fence or guard, access control); (d) fire-authority written approval of pre-treatment hazards; (e) insurer letter confirming on-site coverage; (f) staff liaison identified and trained; (g) data connectivity (fiber or satellite ≥10 Mbps). Each criterion is scored ready/not-ready/in-progress. Begin readiness coordination 6 months before scheduled unit arrival. A unit is dispatched only when all criteria are ready. Publish scorecard status monthly. Budget 1–2 FTE for Site Readiness Coordinator.

8. Define escalation thresholds and governance triggers for cost overruns, schedule slips and technical failures.

The plan identifies risks but does not specify at what variance a decision escalates to the Programme Board (5%? 10%? 20%?) or what actions result (pause, rework, governance re-assessment, go/no-go). Without clear triggers, cost and schedule variances accumulate silently until a crisis forces an emergency meeting.

Recommendation: By Month 2 (2026-12-12), publish an Escalation and Governance Triggers Document specifying: (a) cumulative overspend >10% on any phase → halt that phase and conduct cost audit; (b) schedule slip >4 weeks → convene schedule-recovery task force; (c) uptime <90% for 2 consecutive months → root-cause investigation and corrective action required before continued operations; (d) any AI metric (precision, recall, flagging) outside acceptable range → governance decision on model retraining or workflow redesign; (e) two or more similar equipment failures across the fleet → design-review investigation. Establish a monthly Variance Review meeting (Programme Director, financial officer, technical lead) reporting to the Programme Board quarterly. Budget for monthly cost and schedule tracking.

9. Develop a supplier and vendor management strategy for 300–500 vintage machines, parts, and 3D-printing services.

The plan sources vintage equipment from eBay, auctions and decommissioned facilities but does not name suppliers, negotiate volume discounts, or document procurement procedures. Without a supplier strategy, acquisitions are reactive and inefficient, and critical parts may become unavailable if a key supplier exits.

Recommendation: By Month 2 (2026-12-12), establish a Vintage Equipment Procurement Team tasked with: (a) mapping major decommissioned broadcast and film equipment suppliers (auctions, facility closures, salvage yards) in North America and Europe; (b) negotiating volume commitments (target 300–500 units at average USD 3–5K per deck/scanner); (c) documenting condition assessment and parts-harvest protocols; (d) establishing relationships with 2–3 specialist 3D-printing and CNC shops for precision-parts fabrication. By Month 4 (2027-02-12), secure written agreements with top-3 suppliers and begin acquisition. Track inventory and supplier reliability monthly. Budget USD 500K–1M for procurement coordination and supplier relationship management.

1.4.A Issue - Parts Depletion Curve and Hardware Sustainment Model Are Speculative, Not Validated

The plan assumes a finite stockpile of 300–500 vintage tape decks and film scanners will sustain 30 units over a decade at >90% uptime. No parts-depletion curve, mean-time-between-failures (MTBF) model, or 3D-printing fabrication validation exists. Without this modeling by Month 2 (2026-12-12), the uptime target is speculative. By Months 36–48 (2029-10-12 to 2030-10-12), parts inventory may approach critical depletion while retired mentors (aged 70–80) age further, risking cascade failures across the fleet. The $250M cap absorbs no emergency stockpile refresh (estimated $15–25M unbudgeted).

  • hardware_sustainment_risk

1.4.C Mitigation

By Month 2 (2026-12-12), commission a Parts Depletion Curve model: specify MTBF per deck type, cannibalization yield per 10 units, and 3D-printing capacity for 20+ critical parts. By Month 4 (2027-02-12), validate fabrication of 10 priority parts on reference decks, measuring playback fidelity against archival standards. By Month 6 (2027-04-12), conduct comprehensive condition assessment of all 300–500 machines and establish a Parts Consumption Telemetry dashboard by Month 10 (2027-08-12) to trigger re-manufacture orders at 50% depletion. This prevents surprise stockouts and provides credible evidence for Phase 2 gates.

1.4.D Consequence

Without modeling, the fleet risks dropping below 90% uptime by Months 36–48 (2029-10-12 to 2030-10-12) as parts inventory depletes and mentors exit. This cascades into missed digitization targets and forced operational pauses. An unbudgeted emergency stockpile refresh ($15–25M) would breach the $250M cap or trigger phase delays while media continues degrading. Archive partnerships may terminate if uptime falls and collections are left unprocessed.

5.4.A Issue - Unvalidated AI Pre-Screening Accuracy Drives Crew Headcount and Budget—Test Real Content Immediately

The plan assumes 80% review reduction (20% content flagged) as a cost-driver anchor, but this is untested on degraded, multilingual, pre-digital content. If actual flagging is 35-40%, reviewer headcount triples from 12-15 to 40-50 per unit, adding USD 15-25M annual payroll at full scale—far exceeding the USD 25M average annual budget envelope. The claim rests on AI precision and recall thresholds (≥75%) that have never been measured on the target dataset. Pilot data by Month 8 (2027-06-12) cannot be deferred; crew composition and Phase 2 approval hinge on this evidence.

5.4.B Tags

  • ai_accuracy_unvalidated
  • review_bottleneck_unproven
  • budget_reconciliation_broken
  • crew_headcount_fragile

5.4.C Mitigation

By Month 4 (2027-02-12), create a gold-standard labeled dataset: 100-200 samples across Tape, Film and Card lines, heavily degraded items, multiple languages. Have 3-5 expert human reviewers independently flag copyright, PII and classification markers; measure inter-rater agreement (Cohen's kappa ≥0.75). Test the AI pre-screening pipeline; publish precision, recall and false-positive rates by category-format-degradation. If any metric <75%, commission iterative retraining before touching real collections. By Month 8 (2027-06-12), measure actual review rates in the pilot pod: flagging percentage and mean hours per content hour. If flagging exceeds 25% or precision <75%, redesign crew model or retrain AI before Phase 2 scale-up. Engage an independent ML validation specialist (not the AI team) to audit results.

5.4.D Consequence

If this validation is deferred or skipped: Phase 2 crew composition will be miscalibrated. If actual flagging is 35-40%, the program will either underfund reviewers (leading to quality failures and privacy incidents) or overfund them (consuming USD 15-25M above budget, forcing unit-count reduction to ≤18 across all phases). Either path breaks the 3.6M-item target or the USD 250M cap. A privacy or copyright false-negative on degraded content could destroy archive partnerships network-wide. Pilot results will lack credibility with funders and archives if this evidence is missing.

5.4.E Root Cause

The plan was designed around an operational assumption (80% review reduction) rather than measured ground truth. No labeled validation dataset from real 1950-2000 content exists; no baseline precision, recall or false-positive rates per content category (copyright, PII, classification) and degradation level have been established. The assumption was never tested and was never meant to be a planning input per the assessment notes, yet it was used as one.

5.5.A Issue - Hardware Sustainment Model Lacks Depletion Curve—Finite Spares Will Exhaust by Month 36-48 (2029-10-12 to 2030-10-12) Without Modeling

The plan depends on a 300-500 vintage-deck stockpile, sustained by cannibalization, to keep 30 units running at >90% uptime for 10 years. Yet no parts-depletion curve, mean-time-between-failures (MTBF) model per deck type, or re-manufacture yield exists. Without this modeling, the uptime target is speculative. Spares will be consumed by continuous operation; once depletion crosses 50%, MTBF and availability worsen sharply. Retired mentors (aged 70-80 now) cannot be held beyond Month 48 (2030-10-12), so knowledge and repair capacity exit before Phase 3 reaches full scale at Month 90-120 (2034-04-12 to 2036-10-12). A mid-program emergency re-purchase of vintage machines (USD 15-25M) may be unavoidable but unbudgeted.

5.5.B Tags

  • spares_depletion_unmapped
  • uptime_target_unsupported
  • mentor_attrition_risk
  • mtbf_not_modeled
  • phase3_feasibility_fragile

5.5.C Mitigation

By Month 2 (2026-12-12), commission a Parts Depletion Model (external specialist, not internal team): for each of the 3 line types, document at least 10 reference machines' MTBF distributions (time-to-failure curves), measured or sourced from broadcast-industry literature. Model spares yield: how many usable parts per 10 machines cannibalized, by part category (heads, transports, motors, belts, optical assemblies). Estimate monthly consumption per active unit and cumulative depletion curve for 160 unit-years (Phase 1-3). Identify the inflection point where remaining spares drop to 50% (the re-manufacture trigger). By Month 4 (2027-02-12), validate 3D-printing and CNC fabrication on at least 10 priority part types by testing on reference-grade decks; measure playback fidelity (azimuth offset, dropout rate, signal-to-noise) against archival standards. By Month 1 (2026-11-12), secure written contracts with 6-8 retired mentors; offer 24-month engagement through Month 24 (2028-10-12), with extension incentive (consulting role, part-time contract) through Month 48 (2030-10-12). Document all mentor knowledge in permanent video and written protocols by Month 4 (2027-02-12). By Month 10 (2027-08-12), deploy a Parts Consumption Telemetry dashboard: each unit logs parts usage monthly; central system triggers re-manufacture orders at 50% depletion threshold. If the depletion model shows infeasible exhaustion (spares fully consumed before Month 100 = 2035-02-12), escalate to governance for go/no-go re-assessment.

5.5.D Consequence

Without a depletion model, the program will experience unplanned stockouts, causing MIU downtime and uptime <90% by Months 36-48 (2029-10-12 to 2030-10-12). This will trigger emergency vintage re-purchase (USD 15-25M unbudgeted), reducing Phase 3 scope or requiring new funding that may not materialize on-time. Mentor knowledge will be lost between Months 24-48 (2028-10-12 to 2030-10-12) as mentors age out or become unavailable; Phase 3 repairs will rely on partially-trained younger engineers, increasing repair time and reducing uptime further. Archive partners will lose confidence if uptime drops below 90%; partnerships could terminate. The stress-first pilot (first unit on worst-condition collection) will expose this risk by Month 12-18 (2027-10-12 to 2028-04-12), but late discovery wastes time and capital.

5.5.E Root Cause

The sustainment strategy was designed conceptually (buy stockpile, cannibalize, retrain engineers) without engineering rigor. No quantitative model of consumption was created. MTBF per deck type and line (Tape, Film, Card) vary widely; some units will fail within 6 months of continuous use, others within 3 years. The yield of usable parts per cannibalized machine is unknown. The 3D-printing and CNC capability is acknowledged but not validated for critical parts (azimuth fixtures, capstan sleeves, pinch rollers). Retired mentors, once engaged, have limited availability windows (18-24 months of intensive work); their exit by Month 48 (2030-10-12) leaves Phase 3 (Months 60-120 = 2031-10-12 to 2036-10-12) operating with younger engineers trained by now-absent mentors.

5.6.A Issue - Budget Reconciliation Unresolved—Recomputed Costs USD 530M vs. Cap USD 250M; Staffing Model Internally Inconsistent

The plan states 50-60 staff per unit at USD 2-3M opex per unit-year. Recomputation shows: payroll alone at 50-60 staff × USD 50-70K loaded cost = USD 2.5-4.2M per unit annually. At full scale (1,500-1,800 staff), annual payroll alone is USD 75-126M, dwarfing the USD 25M average annual budget envelope. Total unconstrained cost is approximately USD 530M (capex USD 105M + equipment USD 20M + training USD 5M + opex 160 unit-years × USD 2.5M = USD 398.75M). This leaves an unfunded gap of approximately USD 280M before contingency and risk add-ons. The Phase 1 and Phase 2 budgets have marginal headroom; Phase 3 is severely underfunded. No reconciliation path is clear: either unit count must drop to ~14-18 (breaking the 3.6M-item target), staffing per unit must halve (breaking quality and training promises), host cost-sharing must materialize (unquantified), or new funders must cover USD 280M+ (uncertain).

5.6.B Tags

  • budget_gap_enormous
  • staffing_model_inconsistent
  • cost_audit_missing
  • phase3_unaffordable
  • scope_target_at_risk

5.6.C Mitigation

By Month 1 (2026-11-12), commission an independent cost audit (external infrastructure or systems consultant, not program staff): item-by-item opex per MIU over 12 months, specifying labor roles and loaded costs per region (Northern Virginia, UK, Netherlands, Australia, Japan—weighted average), equipment consumables per line type, satellite/fiber uplink, depreciation, contingency. Publish three scenarios (baseline, +15% inflation, +30% inflation) for Months 0-120 (2026-10-12 to 2036-10-12). By Month 3 (2027-01-12), run a pilot staffing pod (first hub site, representative crew) and measure actual loaded costs over 3 months; extrapolate to full scale. By Month 4 (2027-02-12), publish a reconciled budget and staffing model locked for Phase 1: specify the funding gap (approximately USD 280M, before reserves) and present three path options: (A) host cost-sharing + new funders close gap; (B) reduce unit count to 14-18 (Phase 3 only ~8-12 units), revise targets to 1.7M items and ~95 PB, replan phases; (C) reduce crew per unit to 25-30 (budget-consistent), accept lower review coverage or longer residencies. Present trigger thresholds: if cost audit shows gap >USD 300M or reconciled staffing forces <20 units, escalate to governance for go/no-go re-assessment. By Month 3 (2027-01-12), establish a Funding Commitment Registry: translate each funder pledge into binding multi-year contract language; target ≥USD 30M committed (not pledged) for Phase 1 and ≥USD 84M (70%) for Phase 2 before that phase launches.

5.6.D Consequence

If this reconciliation is deferred or glossed over, Phase 1 will be underfunded (estimated ~USD 14.5M headroom against ~USD 16-28.5M in risk add-ons and inflation), forcing cost cuts mid-execution. Staffing will be inadequate relative to crew-role promises, leading to quality failures, mentor overload, and burnout. Phase 2 approval gates will not hold credibly if the budget arithmetic is visibly broken; funders will demand answers before releasing tranches. Phase 3 will be wholly unaffordable without material changes (fewer units, reduced scope, or new funding); media degradation will continue while governance re-assesses. The plan will lose strategic credibility with archives, insurers and government partners if budget and staffing are perceived as unresolved assumptions rather than realistic plans. Pilot evidence will be discounted if the financial base is unstable.

5.6.E Root Cause

The plan was architected on two untested assumptions: (1) the stated staffing of 50-60 per unit would fit USD 2-3M opex, and (2) the USD 250M cap was sufficient to deliver 30 units and 3.6M items. Neither assumption was cost-modeled at origination. When recomputed, the figures do not reconcile: staffing is undersized relative to the stated crew roles (3-4 engineers + maintenance, 12-15 reviewers, logistics liaison = ~20 minimum operational core; adding pre-treatment, robotics, QC, data-transmission staff yields 40+ easily). Equally, the cap was set as a policy constraint, not derived from bottom-up cost buildup. The two constraints are now in collision.
