Failure Modes

FM1 - The Phantom Pledge Cliff

  • Archetype: Process/Financial
  • Root Cause: Assumption A1
  • Owner: Programme Director and Finance Lead
  • Risk Level: CRITICAL 25/25 (Likelihood 5/5 × Impact 5/5)
Failure Story
  • Plan lists funders without binding commitment mechanisms.
  • Payroll recomputed at USD 75-126M per year at full scale (estimate) against a USD 25M average annual budget.
  • Phase 1 procurement locks in headcount and units before reconciliation.
  • Phase 2 tranche slips; bridge facility is drained.
  • Phase 3 gap of about USD 301M (estimate) has no source; the network stalls near 14 units.
Early Warning Signs
  • Committed funds below USD 30M at Month 3 (2027-01-12)
  • Independent cost audit not delivered by Month 1 (2026-11-12)
  • Funders request annual re-approval of multi-year pledges
  • Host cost-share letters received from fewer than 5 of 10 surveyed sites
Tripwires
  • Committed (not pledged) Phase 1 funds < USD 30M at Month 3 (2027-01-12)
  • Cumulative cost variance >= 10% overspend in any phase
  • Phase 2 commitments < USD 84M (70%) at Month 20 (2028-06-12)
Response Playbook
  • Contain: Freeze new long-lead procurement and hiring beyond the three pilots; draw only from the contingency and bridge facility under Board signature.
  • Assess: Commission the independent audit to rebuild cost per unit-year, quantify the committed-versus-pledged gap, and model 14, 18 and 24 unit scenarios within 4 weeks.
  • Respond: Re-baseline scope to the funded unit count, renegotiate gates with funders, and pursue cost-share or new funders before releasing any further capex.

STOP RULE: If committed funding covers fewer than 24 units' worth of reconciled cost by Month 24 (2028-10-12), halt Phase 2 and re-scope the programme to the funded unit count.

FM2 - The Last Capstan Sleeve

  • Archetype: Technical/Logistical
  • Root Cause: Assumption A2
  • Owner: Vintage Equipment Sustainment Engineer / Parts Manager
  • Risk Level: CRITICAL 20/25 (Likelihood 4/5 × Impact 5/5)
Failure Story
  • No MTBF model or cannibalization yield exists.
  • Continuous 24/7 operation consumes finite heads, transports and motors.
  • 3D-printed parts miss azimuth and speed tolerances; a bad part damages a unique tape.
  • Mentors aged 70-80 exit before successors are certified.
  • Units idle for weeks awaiting parts; uptime falls below 90%; emergency refresh of USD 15-25M (estimate) is unbudgeted.
Early Warning Signs
  • Provisional parts-depletion model (literature MTBF and inventory baseline) not delivered by Month 2 (2026-12-12), or validated model (after bench test and 3D-print tolerance results) not delivered by Month 4-5 (2027-02-12 to 2027-03-12)
  • Fabricated parts fail playback fidelity tests on reference decks
  • Mentor contracts unsigned or a mentor unavailable for over 60 days
  • Repeated identical failure signatures across units in one week
Tripwires
  • Spares inventory <= 50% of baseline for any critical part category (re-manufacture trigger at 50% spares depletion, confirmed only once the validated model exists at Month 4-5 (2027-02-12 to 2027-03-12); proposed threshold)
  • Trailing 6-month fleet uptime < 90%
  • Fewer than 6 signed mentor contracts at Month 1 (2026-11-12)
Response Playbook
  • Contain: Quarantine suspect fabricated parts, pause affected decks, and move cannibalization of working machines under written sign-off.
  • Assess: Re-run the depletion model with measured field MTBF and yield, and rank part categories by weeks of cover remaining.
  • Respond: Trigger re-manufacture or vendor sourcing, activate extended mentor consulting contracts, and re-plan unit schedule or request emergency stockpile funding.

STOP RULE: If the validated model shows spares exhausted before Month 100 (2035-02-12) at the funded unit count, cancel further unit builds and pivot to the vendor-operated model.

FM3 - The Leak That Closed the Doors

  • Archetype: Market/Human
  • Root Cause: Assumption A3
  • Owner: AI Signal Processing and Metadata Engineering Lead
  • Risk Level: CRITICAL 20/25 (Likelihood 4/5 × Impact 5/5)
Failure Story
  • Assumed 80% review reduction fails on degraded, multilingual content.
  • Reviewers burn out under 35-40% flagging; backlog builds.
  • Under pressure, thresholds loosen and a false negative uploads personal data.
  • Archives and insurers read it as breach of trust.
  • Host agreements are suspended; funders question the gates; the network shrinks.
Early Warning Signs
  • Flagging above 25% in the pilot review pod
  • Reviewer turnover above 20% annually
  • Backlog exceeds 4 weeks of on-board storage
  • Privacy false-negative rate above 5% in audit samples
Tripwires
  • AI precision or recall < 75% on any category-format pair
  • Flagging rate > 25% over 4 consecutive weeks
  • Review hours per content hour > 0.5
Response Playbook
  • Contain: Hold all uploads of affected categories, keep content in the restricted tier, and notify the host archive within 24 hours.
  • Assess: Audit a stratified sample of passed items, measure false negatives by format and language, and review decision logs with the Privacy Review Panel.
  • Respond: Retrain or redesign the review workflow, rebuild crew sizing, and brief archives, insurers and funders openly before resuming uploads.

STOP RULE: If privacy false-negative rate stays above 5% after one retraining cycle, or any reportable privacy incident occurs, suspend uploads and trigger governance re-assessment.

FM4 - The Insurer's Veto

  • Archetype: Process/Financial
  • Root Cause: Assumption A4
  • Owner: Risk and Legal Lead
  • Risk Level: CRITICAL 16/25 (Likelihood 4/5 × Impact 4/5)
Failure Story
  • Pilot design assumes on-site pre-treatment is insurable.
  • Insurer quotes exclude ovens and generators or demand detached pods.
  • Pod retrofit (USD 0.5-1.5M each) and 4-6 weeks per site drain the thin contingency.
  • Approval delays push Unit 1 past Month 6 (2027-04-12), compressing pilot evidence before the Month 24 (2028-10-12) gate.
  • Premiums rise after any incident, and fleet-wide pods (USD 15-45M) (estimate) are unfunded.
Early Warning Signs
  • No insurer written feedback by Month 3 (2027-01-12)
  • Broker quotes list exclusions for thermal or chemical events
  • Fire authority requests a separation distance above the host hardstand
  • Pooled loss reserve of USD 2-5M (estimate) not funded
Tripwires
  • No written insurer approval at any pilot site by Month 6 (2027-04-12)
  • Approval conditions add >= 4 weeks per site
  • Annual premium quote exceeds USD 1M (proposed threshold)
Response Playbook
  • Contain: Stop site-specific retrofit spending and hold Unit 1 shipment until approval conditions are written down.
  • Assess: Cost the detached-pod, reduced-intake and self-insured reserve options per site and per unit with the broker within 3 weeks.
  • Respond: Adopt the cheapest approvable option, update the Hazard Control Standard, and re-baseline pilot dates and Phase 1 contingency with the Board.

STOP RULE: If no insurer and fire authority approve any pre-treatment design by Month 9 (2027-07-12), cancel on-site pre-treatment and pivot to host-cold-storage deferral or fixed-site conservation labs.

FM5 - The Container in Customs Limbo

  • Archetype: Technical/Logistical
  • Root Cause: Assumption A5
  • Owner: Site Operations and Logistics Coordinator
  • Risk Level: HIGH 12/25 (Likelihood 3/5 × Impact 4/5)
Failure Story
  • Temporary-admission paperwork for obsolete electronics and hazmat consumables is untested.
  • Vintage decks are classed as e-waste; consumables need hazmat transport.
  • A unit idles in port for weeks, losing throughput and host residency windows.
  • Host-country residency rules block upload, forcing separate in-country storage.
  • Schedule slips cascade across residencies and the 15,600 items per unit-year requirement is missed (estimate).
Early Warning Signs
  • Customs pathway document not complete by Month 4 (2027-02-12)
  • Broker flags e-waste classification for vintage decks
  • Regulator will not confirm permitted replica locations in writing
  • First relocation paperwork takes longer than 6 weeks
Tripwires
  • Any unit idle in transit >= 14 days
  • Fewer than 3 temporary-import agreements by Month 6 (2027-04-12)
  • Share of units blocked by customs holds >= 10% (proposed threshold)
Response Playbook
  • Contain: Pause cross-border moves and re-route units to domestic or same-bloc hosts while paperwork is cleared.
  • Assess: Map each stuck item by classification, regulator and cost per idle day, and test data-residency options with counsel.
  • Respond: Concentrate the next 5 residencies in one customs bloc, adopt regional storage with in-country masters, and re-sequence the master schedule.

STOP RULE: If more than 2 of the first 5 target countries refuse temporary admission by Month 12 (2027-10-12), restrict the fleet to one customs bloc and re-scope the unit and country targets.

FM6 - The Archives That Said No

  • Archetype: Market/Human
  • Root Cause: Assumption A6
  • Owner: Privacy, Rights and Legal Compliance Officer
  • Risk Level: CRITICAL 16/25 (Likelihood 4/5 × Impact 4/5)
Failure Story
  • Archives want guaranteed perpetual storage and no training-data use.
  • Technology funders expect research or training access to recover value.
  • Source agreements stall; the most endangered collections are not released.
  • Rights holders or press frame the program as a data grab.
  • Pilot hosts withdraw, funders hesitate, and the fleet lacks enough host sites.
Early Warning Signs
  • Archive counsel returns agreements with exclusivity or storage clauses
  • Technology funder drafts require training-data rights
  • Fewer than 10 archives engage in the stakeholder workshop
  • Public criticism of data-access terms in sector press
Tripwires
  • Fewer than 3 signed pilot agreements by Month 6 (2027-04-12)
  • More than 30% of candidates request a named storage steward (proposed threshold)
  • A funder term conflicts with source-agreement terms at signature
Response Playbook
  • Contain: Suspend technology-sector funder talks and freeze new data-access commitments until the policy is signed by archives.
  • Assess: Interview each declining archive to rank objections by cost, rights, trust and storage, and quantify capacity lost.
  • Respond: Publish a research-only, rights-holder-approved Data-Access Policy, offer archive-held masters, and secure a named stewardship commitment.

STOP RULE: If fewer than 2 pilot archives sign by Month 9 (2027-07-12) without terms the program cannot honour, halt the pilot build and redesign the partnership model.

FM7 - The Mentors Who Ran Out of Time

  • Archetype: Market/Human
  • Root Cause: Assumption A7
  • Owner: Vintage Equipment Sustainment Engineer / Parts Manager
  • Risk Level: CRITICAL 16/25 (Likelihood 4/5 × Impact 4/5)
Failure Story
  • Mentors aged 70-80 are perishable; contracts are unsigned or short.
  • Reviewers burn out; turnover forces constant onboarding.
  • Successors are under-trained when a mentor exits before Month 18 (2028-04-12).
  • Field failures go undiagnosed; consultant fees rise to USD 5-10K per incident (estimate).
  • Uptime and review quality fall together.
Early Warning Signs
  • Mentor contracts unsigned at Month 1 (2026-11-12)
  • Successor competency sign-offs behind curriculum plan
  • Reviewer attrition above 20% annualised
  • Mentor unavailable for over 60 days
Tripwires
  • Signed mentor contracts < 6 at Month 1 (2026-11-12)
  • Reviewer turnover >= 20% annualised
  • Successor competency sign-offs < 50% of plan at Month 18 (2028-04-12)
Response Playbook
  • Contain: Freeze solo repairs by unsigned successors and route all faults to the remaining mentors with written logs.
  • Assess: Map competencies per line type against surviving mentors and rank single-points-of-failure within 3 weeks.
  • Respond: Extend retention contracts to Month 54 (2031-04-12), recruit backup mentors and add paid cross-training overlap.

STOP RULE: If fewer than 2 mentors per line type remain under contract at Month 24 (2028-10-12), halt Phase 2 unit builds until succession is certified.

FM8 - The Board That Could Not Decide

  • Archetype: Process/Financial
  • Root Cause: Assumption A8
  • Owner: Programme Director
  • Risk Level: HIGH 12/25 (Likelihood 3/5 × Impact 4/5)
Failure Story
  • Decision rights across funders and archives are undefined.
  • Gate and site-priority decisions take 8-12 weeks each.
  • Funders pull terms toward their own collections or data access.
  • Tranche releases slip; the bridge facility is drawn.
  • Phase 2 starts late and calendar is lost against media decay.
Early Warning Signs
  • Governance charter not ratified by Month 2 (2026-12-12)
  • Repeated deferral of agenda items
  • Funder side letters conflicting with Board decisions
  • Gate evidence waiting on Board review
Tripwires
  • Routine decision cycle >= 4 weeks
  • Charter unsigned at Month 2 (2026-12-12)
  • Phase 2 gate decision pending > 8 weeks after evidence
Response Playbook
  • Contain: Delegate routine decisions to named committees with a 10-day clock and pause contested items.
  • Assess: Log every pending decision, owner, age and funder dependency within 2 weeks.
  • Respond: Amend the charter with tie-break rules and publish site-priority criteria agreed in writing by all funders.

STOP RULE: If the Phase 2 gate decision is not taken within 12 weeks of complete evidence, trigger an external governance review and suspend new commitments.

FM9 - The Buffer That Filled Overnight

  • Archetype: Technical/Logistical
  • Root Cause: Assumption A9
  • Owner: Central Operations and Fleet Management Officer
  • Risk Level: HIGH 12/25 (Likelihood 3/5 × Impact 4/5)
Failure Story
  • Capture rate outruns host uplink and verification.
  • 500 TB on-board buffer fills; units stop capturing.
  • Fixity failures force re-transfer and re-verification.
  • Backlog blocks relocation and idles scarce decks.
  • Two-copy target is missed and archives lose confidence.
Early Warning Signs
  • Measured uplink below planned daily volume
  • Buffer above 60% for a week
  • Fixity-check failures above 1% of files
  • Host link outages longer than 24 hours
Tripwires
  • On-board buffer >= 80% for 14 consecutive days
  • Fixity failure rate >= 1% of files
  • Upload backlog >= 4 weeks
Response Playbook
  • Contain: Throttle intake to the verified drain rate and stage derivatives for upload first.
  • Assess: Measure link capacity, verification speed and failure causes per site within 2 weeks.
  • Respond: Add offline media deposit or a federated copy path, upgrade links, and resize buffer in the Phase 2 design.

STOP RULE: If buffer-driven stoppages exceed 10% of unit-months across the pilots, freeze Phase 2 design until the data path is redesigned.

Reality check: fix before go.

Summary

Level Count Explanation
🛑 High 12 Existential blocker without credible mitigation.
⚠️ Medium 5 Material risk with plausible path.
✅ Low 3 Minor/controlled risk.

Checklist

1. Violates Known Physics

Does the plan's success require breaking a known law of physics (e.g., thermodynamics, conservation of energy, speed-of-light limit, causality)?

Level: ✅ Low

Justification: This is a project-management and engineering plan to deploy mobile digitization containers to preserve degraded media through electromechanical scanning, digital signal processing, and archival storage. All mechanisms—robotic loading, audio/video signal reconstruction, optical scanning, parts cannibalization, human-supervised AI review, and materials conservation—operate within established physics and do not require violating conservation laws, speed-of-light limits, causality, or other named physics constraints. The plan acknowledges real engineering challenges (equipment scarcity, timeline, budget, design validation) but does not depend on any non-physical causal mechanism.

Mitigation: No physics-related action required — the plan does not invoke physics-incompatible mechanisms.

2. No Real-World Proof

Does success depend on a technology or system that has not been proven in real projects at this scale or in this domain?

Level: 🛑 High

Justification: Rated HIGH because the plan hinges on a novel combination of obsolete equipment sustainment (finite 300–500 vintage machine stockpile, retired-engineer mentoring, 3D-printed parts at ±0.05mm tolerance), unvalidated AI pre-screening accuracy (claimed 80% review reduction on degraded, multilingual 1950–2000 content), unprecedented mobile containerized digitization at 30 sites across multiple jurisdictions, and a staffing model (50–60 per unit) that does not reconcile with the stated USD 2–3M opex per unit-year. The plan bans 'assumptions about equipment availability' yet depends entirely on: (1) no alternative source for 300–500 decommissioned decks if primary sources dry up; (2) fabricated parts meeting archival playback tolerances without fail; (3) six to eight mentors (ages 70–80) remaining available and medically able through Month 48 (2030-10-12) with no named successors vetted; (4) AI pre-screening precision and recall ≥75% on content the model has never seen; (5) institutional trust surviving any handling incident or privacy breach; (6) archive partnerships persisting if perpetual-storage stewardship is not named by Month 36 (2029-10-12). No independent evidence at comparable scale exists for this integrated system. Vendor-operated digitization (Industry precedent: Indiana University MDPI with Memnon) succeeds for outsourced work but not for embedded knowledge transfer. Standalone vintage equipment restoration exists (Library of Congress Packard Campus) but at fixed sites, not mobile. Multi-site archival networks with human rights review exist (British Library Unlocking Our Sound Heritage) but not with vintage equipment, on-site pre-treatment, or unproven AI. The closest analogue—Indiana MDPI—was fixed-facility, vendor-operated, single-format (audio/video) and did not include containerized transport, overseas deployment or 30+ simultaneous sites. Failure in any critical subdomand (parts availability, mentor attrition, AI accuracy, institutional trust) would be existential: uptime collapses, crew quality fails, partnerships terminate, funder confidence erodes, and media degradation accelerates unrecovered.

Mitigation: Establish six parallel validation tracks, each with defined NO-GO gates and independent third-party sign-off: (1) Hardware Sustainment Track: Commission parts-depletion model (MTBF per deck, cannibalization yield, 3D-printing tolerance validation on reference decks) by Month 2 (2026-12-12); confirm no unplanned stockouts in pilot operations by Month 12 (2027-10-12); NO-GO gate: spares inventory <50% before Month 60 (2031-10-12) or fabricated parts miss azimuth tolerance ±0.05mm. (2) AI Accuracy Track: Procure 100–200 representative degraded samples from three pilot archives; build gold-standard labeled dataset (inter-rater agreement Cohen's kappa ≥0.75) by Month 4 (2027-02-12); measure precision/recall ≥75% per category-format-degradation by Month 8 (2027-06-12); Trigger ladder (proposed threshold): precision or recall <75% or flagging >25% -> retrain/recalibrate; flagging >30% -> redesign review workflow; <70% after retraining -> governance re-assessment; false-negative privacy rate >5% after one retraining cycle is also a NO-GO. (3) Budget-Cost Reconciliation Track: Commission independent cost audit itemizing opex per unit-year (labor, equipment, consumables) and model three scenarios (2%, 3% and 4% annual escalation, about 22% / 34% / 48% cumulative by Month 120 = 2036-10-12) by Month 4 (2027-02-12); lock staffing model (50–60 per unit vs. budget-consistent ~25) and reconcile to cap; NO-GO gate: reconciled cost exceeds USD 250M cap for stated scope by >10%, or only ~14 units are fundable (triggering scope reduction trigger). (4) Mentor and Staffing Track: Secure written 24-month contracts with 6–8 retired broadcast engineers (min 2 per line type) by Month 1 (2026-11-12); develop mentoring curriculum and competency milestones by Month 4 (2027-02-12); validate successor competency sign-offs by Month 30 (2029-04-12); NO-GO gate: fewer than 6 mentors under contract, >20% reviewer turnover annualized, or <50% of successor engineers certified. (5) Legal/Privacy/Institutional-Trust Track: Map jurisdiction-specific data-protection law (GDPR, UK DPA, local rules) by Month 1 (2026-11-12); publish standardized source-agreement template with privacy and tiered-indemnity terms by Month 3 (2027-01-12); secure written insurer and fire-authority approval at one pilot site by Month 6 (2027-04-12); NO-GO gate: no insurer approval at any site by Month 9 (2027-07-12), or any privacy breach; host tripwire: <3 host archives signed by Month 6 (2027-04-12), stop if <2 by Month 9 (2027-07-12). (6) Funder-Commitment and Funding-Gap Track: Establish Funding Commitment Registry by Month 1 (2026-11-12); convert ≥50% of Phase 1 (USD 30M) from pledges to binding contracts by Month 3 (2027-01-12); identify backup sources (host cost-share, new funders, technology-sector licensing) to close the ~USD 280M Phase 3 gap; NO-GO gate: committed funds <USD 30M for Phase 1, or Phase 2 commitments <USD 84M (70%) by Month 20 (2028-06-12), or no identified funding path for Phase 3 by Month 36 (2029-10-12). Two Global NO-GO Gates: (A) Empirical/Engineering Validity: If any track (parts, AI, staffing, budget) fails its validation gate, trigger immediate governance escalation; defer Phase 2 release until remediation is complete (retraining 2–4 weeks, design rework 6–9 months, or scope reduction to fundable unit count). (B) Legal/Compliance Clearance: If fire authority or insurer approval is denied at all three pilot sites by Month 9 (2027-07-12), or if <2 archive agreements are signed by Month 9 (2027-07-12), or if any reportable privacy incident occurs, halt all new deployments and conduct governance re-assessment. Reject Domain-Mismatched PoCs: Do not validate AI accuracy using clean, digitally-born test data; only degraded, multilingual 1950–2000 samples represent real content. Do not defer parts model to Phase 2; MTBF and fabrication tolerance must be locked by Month 2 (2026-12-12). Do not accept vendor precedent (e.g., Memnon with Indiana MDPI) as proof of mobile, multi-site, on-site-pre-treatment viability; independently test hazard control and insurer approval. Owner / Deliverable / Date: Programme Director and Finance Lead own Tracks 3, 5, 6 (budget, legal, funding); Chief Engineer owns Tracks 1, 2, 4 (hardware, AI, mentors). Each track produces one authoritative third-party audit or supervised pilot result. All six tracks must sign off by Month 8 (2027-06-12); if any track remains unvalidated, Phase 2 release is held and scope/timeline/crew are re-baselined by Month 24 (2028-10-12) governance decision.

3. Buzzwords

Does the plan use excessive buzzwords without evidence of knowledge?

Level: 🛑 High

Justification: Rated HIGH because the plan names 15 strategic decisions (Vintage Transport Sustainment Strategy, Rights/Privacy/Review Gate Design, Crew Composition, Funding and Ownership Architecture, Pilot Proof Gates, Triage Doctrine, Custody/Format/Access Regime, Restoration Intervention Ceiling, Pre-Treatment Hazard Design, Host-Site Power/Security Compact, Recovery Assurance and Independent Verification, Border-Crossing/Data-Jurisdiction Pathway, Liability and Loss-Indemnity Structure, Fleet Command and Remote Diagnostics, Fleet Sunset and Equipment Afterlife) but treats most as open decisions without locked business-level mechanisms. Critical example: Decision 2 (Rights, Privacy, Review Gate Design) states three strategic choices exist but does not specify which is chosen; assumes 80% review reduction as input hypothesis, not measured outcome. Decision 1 (Vintage Transport) names stockpile-plus-mentoring approach but lacks parts-depletion curve (mechanism-of-action undefined). Decision 4 (Funding) lists three routes (consortium, service bureau, technology revenue) without committing to one. No owner or success metric is locked for most decisions before Phase 1 procurement (Month 4 = 2027-02-12). The plan bans 'assumptions about equipment' yet every decision rests on untested assumptions and deferred validation.

Mitigation: By Month 4 (2027-02-12), lock one chosen option per decision (not all three) with explicit owner and measurable outcome: e.g., Decision 2: "Gate all items behind AI pre-screen + human review before upload; Privacy Review Panel owns decisions; success = zero privacy breaches, <20% flagging, AI precision/recall ≥75%." Publish one-pagers per decision (5 pages max each): mechanism-of-action (input→process→customer value), owner, success metric, decision hook (what triggers reconsideration). Owner: Programme Director coordinates with 8-10 Board members; each strategic decision assigned to a named functional lead (Finance, Legal, Chief Engineer, Operations). Deadline: Month 4 (2027-02-12); validate via independent review before Phase 1 procurement.

4. Underestimating Risks

Does this plan grossly underestimate risks?

Level: 🛑 High

Justification: Rated HIGH because the plan assumes AI pre-screening will flag only 20% of content (80% reduction), requiring 12–15 reviewers per unit and driving crew composition to 50–60 staff per MIU. This assumption is untested on degraded, multilingual 1950–2000 content. If actual flagging is 35–40%, reviewer headcount rises about 1.75–2x to roughly 21–30 per unit, adding about USD 14–32M annual payroll at full scale (estimate) and breaching the USD 25M average annual budget envelope. Additionally, the plan lacks a modeled parts-depletion curve for 300–500 vintage machines sustaining 30 units at >90% uptime; mentor knowledge transfer from retired engineers (aged 70–80) is perishable and incompletely documented; perpetual storage of 200+ PB beyond Month 120 (2036-10-12) has no committed steward; and insurer and fire-authority approvals for pre-treatment hazards are unvalidated. Any single failure (AI accuracy <75%, flagging >25%, parts stockout, mentor attrition, privacy breach, institutional-trust loss) cascades into unmet targets and cascade partnership termination. The plan bans 'assumptions about equipment' yet every critical system relies on untested assumptions replaced by pilot evidence only by Month 8 (2027-06-12)—too late to redesign if validation fails.

Mitigation: By Month 2 (2026-12-12), commission six parallel validation tracks with independent third-party sign-off and explicit NO-GO gates: (1) Parts-Depletion Model: Bench-test 10 reference decks for 8–12 weeks; validate 3D-printed tolerance ±0.05mm on 10 parts; NO-GO if spares fall below 50% before Month 60 (2031-10-12). (2) AI Accuracy: Procure 100–200 representative degraded samples; build gold-standard labeled dataset (Cohen's kappa ≥0.75) by Month 4 (2027-02-12); measure precision/recall ≥75% per category-format by Month 8 (2027-06-12); retrain if any metric <75% or flagging >25%; redesign review workflow if flagging >30%; governance re-assessment if <70% after retraining. (3) Budget Reconciliation: Commission independent cost audit reconciling USD 75–126M payroll (estimate) against USD 25M average budget; lock staffing model (25 vs. 50–60 per unit) by Month 4 (2027-02-12); NO-GO if reconciled cost forces <24 units. (4) Mentor Contracts: Secure 6–8 mentors by Month 1 (2026-11-12); document curriculum and competency milestones by Month 4 (2027-02-12); validate successor sign-offs by Month 30 (2029-04-12); NO-GO if <6 mentors or >20% reviewer turnover annualized. (5) Legal/Privacy Compliance: Map GDPR, UK DPA per jurisdiction by Month 1 (2026-11-12); obtain written insurer and fire-authority approval at one pilot site by Month 6 (2027-04-12); sign 3 host agreements by Month 6 (2027-04-12); NO-GO if approval denied at all sites by Month 9 (2027-07-12) or <2 archives signed by Month 9 (2027-07-12) (tripwire <3 by Month 6 = 2027-04-12). (6) Funder Commitment: Establish Registry by Month 1 (2026-11-12); secure ≥USD 30M Phase 1 committed by Month 3 (2027-01-12); identify funding sources for ~USD 280M Phase 3 gap; NO-GO if committed funds <USD 30M Phase 1 or <USD 84M Phase 2 (70%) by Month 20 (2028-06-12). Two Global NO-GO Gates: (A) If any track fails its validation gate, defer Phase 2 release (Month 24 = 2028-10-12) and trigger 2–4 week retraining or 6–9 month design rework. (B) If fire/insurer approval is denied at all pilot sites or any privacy incident occurs, halt deployments and conduct governance re-assessment. Owner: Programme Director (Tracks 3, 5, 6); Chief Engineer (Tracks 1, 2, 4). Each track delivers one third-party audit by Month 8 (2027-06-12); all six must sign off before Phase 2 release or scope/staffing is re-baselined.

5. Timeline Issues

Does the plan rely on unrealistic or internally inconsistent schedules?

Level: ⚠️ Medium

Justification: Rated MEDIUM because critical predecessors (AI validation Month 8 = 2027-06-12, cost reconciliation Month 4 = 2027-02-12, permit approvals Months 2–6 = 2026-12-12 to 2027-04-12, funder commitment Month 3 = 2027-01-12) are interdependent and schedule-critical, but no permit and approval matrix, critical-path network or detailed lead-time validation exists. Phase 2 gate (Month 24 = 2028-10-12) depends on all six predecessors; a 2–4 week slip in any one cascades to 4–8 week Phase 2 delay. Long-lead procurement (containers 12–18 months, equipment TBD, robotics 16+ weeks) is untethered to firm supplier commitments. Phased funding release (annual funder cycles, 4–8 week approval) adds 3–6 month aggregate slip risk. Media degradation timeline (10–30 years) is unmodeled against schedule delays. With explicit permit timeline validation, long-lead LOIs, critical-path analysis and variance escalation thresholds, the schedule becomes plausible; without them, 4–12 month cumulative slips and unmet targets are likely.

Mitigation: Finance Lead and Site Operations Coordinator: Rebuild critical-path Gantt schedule (task-level dependencies, dated predecessors, slack analysis) by Month 1 (2026-11-12). Document permit and approval lead times per jurisdiction (fire, insurer, customs, GDPR) and create regulatory approval matrix by Month 2 (2026-12-12). Secure non-binding long-lead supplier LOIs (containers, robotics, power systems) confirming delivery windows by Month 1 (2026-11-12). Establish variance thresholds (cumulative slip >= 8 weeks = NO-GO gate escalation) and monthly cost/schedule variance dashboard by Month 3 (2027-01-12). Publish critical-path summary to Programme Board and funder consortium monthly.

6. Money Issues

Are there flaws in the financial model, funding plan, or cost realism?

Level: ⚠️ Medium

Justification: Rated MEDIUM because the plan allocates USD 250M across three phases with stated budgets (Phase 1 USD 60M, Phase 2 USD 120M, Phase 3 USD 70M) but funding is only pledged (not committed). Recomputed costs show approximate USD 530M unconstrained, creating an approximate USD 280M unfunded gap before reserves. Phase 3 particularly vulnerable: USD 70M cap minus USD 52.5M for 15 new MIU capex leaves USD 17.5M for 7 unit-years of opex (about 5–6 months of 15-unit operation, estimate); with no new MIUs it would fund 28 unit-years (15 units to about Month 82 = 2033-08-12), both before the USD 7M contingency. Staffing model does not reconcile—USD 75–126M annual payroll at full scale against USD 25M average annual budget. Phase 2 and Phase 3 funding releases are tied to gates but draw schedules and triggering conditions lack documented binding commitment and override protocols. USD 15–20M contingency for phase-transition cash-flow gaps is proposed but not pre-qualified. Perpetual storage beyond Month 120 (2036-10-12) is unbudgeted and lacks named steward.

Mitigation: Finance Lead and Programme Director: By Month 1 (2026-11-12), establish Funding Commitment Registry documenting each of 15+ funders' pledged amount, commitment status (pledged vs. committed), conditions, and release schedule. Convert ≥50% of Phase 1 (USD 30M of USD 60M) from pledges to binding multi-year contracts with explicit milestone-release conditions by Month 3 (2027-01-12). By Month 4 (2027-02-12), publish three budget scenarios (2%, 3% and 4% annual escalation, about 22% / 34% / 48% cumulative by Month 120 = 2036-10-12; the 15% reserve of USD 9M / 18M / 10.5M is a separate proposed provision) and lock staffing model (50–60 per unit vs. budget-consistent ~25 per unit); reconcile cost-to-cap or document scope reduction. Pre-qualify USD 15–20M revolving credit facility by Month 2 (2026-12-12) with 4-6 week drawdown trigger if Phase 2 commitment falls <70% (USD 84M) by Month 20 (2028-06-12). By Month 36 (2029-10-12), secure written commitment from ≥1 national archive for perpetual stewardship of 200+ PB masters and identify post-Month 120 (2036-10-12) funding mechanism (endowment, government pledge, or revenue model). Owner: Finance Lead, with Board sign-off; Deliverable: Dated Funding Commitment Registry, three budget scenarios, and stewardship letter of intent; Date: Within 4 months (Month 4 = 2027-02-12 for scenarios; Month 3 = 2027-01-12 for Phase 1 conversions; Month 36 = 2029-10-12 for stewardship).

7. Budget Too Low

Is there a significant mismatch between the project's stated goals and the financial resources allocated, suggesting an unrealistic or inadequate budget?

Level: 🛑 High

Justification: Rated HIGH because recomputed unconstrained cost is approximately USD 530M against the USD 250M cap, creating an unfunded gap of approximately USD 280M. Staffing model (50–60 per unit at USD 50–70K loaded = USD 2.5–4.2M payroll) does not reconcile with stated opex of USD 2–3M per unit-year; budget-consistent crew is ~25 staff per unit. Phase 3 (USD 70M allocated minus USD 52.5M for 15 new MIUs = USD 17.5M remaining) can fund only 7 unit-years of opex (about 5–6 months of 15-unit operation, estimate), not the full 60-month phase at 15 units; with no new MIUs it would fund 28 unit-years (15 units to about Month 82 = 2033-08-12), both before the USD 7M contingency. No binding commitment mechanism exists to close the gap, and no scope reduction (to ~14 units) or crew-size reduction (to ~25 per unit) is locked before Phase 1 procurement (Month 4 = 2027-02-12).

Mitigation: Finance Lead and Programme Director: By Month 1 (2026-11-12), commission independent cost audit itemizing opex per MIU-year (salaries, benefits, logistics, consumables, parts, utilities). By Month 4 (2027-02-12), publish three budget scenarios (baseline USD 250M vs. recomputed USD 530M; 2%, 3% and 4% annual escalation scenarios) and lock one credible staffing model (50–60 per unit vs. budget-consistent ~25 per unit). Identify and pre-qualify three funding sources (host cost-sharing per MIU, new government or consortium funders, non-exclusive technology-sector licensing) targeting USD 280M gap closure or explicit scope reduction (to ~14–18 unit-equivalents) by Month 4 (2027-02-12). Establish monthly cost-variance dashboard by Month 6 (2027-04-12); escalate >10% cumulative overspend to governance go/no-go decision.

8. Overly Optimistic Projections

Does this plan grossly overestimate the likelihood of success, while neglecting potential setbacks, buffers, or contingency plans?

Level: 🛑 High

Justification: Rated HIGH because key projections (3.6M items, 200+ PB, 30 units by Month 120 = 2036-10-12, >90% uptime, 80% AI review reduction, USD 69 per-item cost) are presented as single-point figures without ranges, confidence intervals, or alternative scenarios. The plan acknowledges failure modes (e.g., "if flagging is 35–40%") but does not publish best/base/worst-case scenarios before Phase 1 procurement locks in crew composition and unit design. The 80% review-reduction assumption drives crew size (12–15 reviewers per unit) and opex credibility; if actual flagging is 35–40%, reviewer headcount rises about 1.75–2x and budget exceeds the cap by roughly USD 14–32M annually (estimate). No contingency scenario is published showing program outcomes at reduced scope (14–18 units instead of 30) or extended timeline (Phase 3 to Month 150 = 2039-04-12 instead of Month 120 = 2036-10-12). The lack of scenario planning obscures downside risk and prevents governance and funders from making informed trade-offs before committing capital in Phase 1.

Mitigation: Programme Director and Finance Lead: By Month 2 (2026-12-12), commission a sensitivity analysis and publish three credible scenarios (Best: AI flagging 15%, parts yield +20%, crew 10–12 per unit, deliver 3.8M items by Month 110 = 2035-12-12; Base: flagging 20%, yield baseline, crew 12–15 per unit, deliver 3.6M by Month 120 = 2036-10-12; Worst: flagging 35%, yield –15%, crew 25–30 per unit or unit count 18 if crew capped, deliver 2.4M by Month 130 = 2037-08-12 or Month 120 = 2036-10-12 at reduced scope). Publish scenarios with explicit cost, schedule and scope trade-offs. Lock gate thresholds that trigger scenario recalibration (e.g., if pilot flagging >25%, initiate Worst-case crew and timeline re-baseline). By Month 4 (2027-02-12), retro-fit gate criteria to reflect scenario ranges, not single-point targets.

9. Lacks Technical Depth

Does the plan omit critical technical details or engineering steps required to overcome foreseeable challenges, especially for complex components of the project?

Level: ✅ Low

Justification: Rated LOW because the plan establishes rigorous engineering specification and validation requirements across all three pilot Mobile Ingest Units (Tape, Film, Card lines) before full fleet replication. The plan explicitly requires: (1) interface contracts specifying container-to-host power/data/climate specifications and MIU-to-archive media handling protocols by Month 4 (2027-02-12); (2) acceptance tests measuring digitization success >95%, reconstruction accuracy >80%, metadata accuracy >70%, uptime >90%, AI pre-screening precision/recall ≥75% per category-format, and zero incidents across ≥2 host sites over ≥3 consecutive months (Months 6-20 = 2027-04-12 to 2028-06-12); (3) detailed integration plan specifying container assembly, site deployment, crew training, and parts replacement workflows with documented owners and dates; (4) non-functional requirements covering thermal stability (±2°C oven tolerance), humidity control (±5% RH), uptime >90% (per the user constraint), latency <4 weeks per relocation, and zero security breaches. The plan names a Design Review Gate (DRG) process (Month 4 = 2027-02-12) and design freeze (Month 20 = 2028-06-12) before Phase 2 long-lead procurement, preventing unvalidated designs from being replicated across 12 Phase 2 units. Mitigation is specified: if pilot thresholds are not met at the Phase 2 gate (Month 24 = 2028-10-12), AI retraining (2-4 weeks), design rework (6-9 months), or scope reduction to fundable units is triggered before Phase 2 release. The plan defers no critical subsystem to later validation: AI accuracy, parts fabrication tolerance, crew composition, insurer/fire-authority approvals, and cost reconciliation are all locked by Month 4 (2027-02-12) via validation gates. Weak point: the Engineering Depth artifacts (interface contracts, detailed integration maps with owner/date pairs for all 30 units' deployments) are sketched as deliverables but not yet created; the plan names them as required but does not show them complete.

Mitigation: Chief Engineer: Create and validate technical specification documents for all three pilot MIUs (Tape, Film, Card lines) by Month 4 (2027-02-12), including (a) detailed container-to-host interface contracts (power: kW/voltage/frequency, data: Mbps/latency, climate: temperature/humidity range, physical: footprint/weight), (b) MIU-to-archive media handling protocols (intake condition grading, pre-treatment sequencing, playback verification, return media packaging), (c) acceptance test plan (sampling rate, measurement instruments, pass/fail thresholds per metric), and (d) integration map specifying each of 30 deployments (site name, arrival month, crew size, residency duration, owner, responsible engineer). Publish design review gate decision (approve designs or defer Phase 2) by Month 20 (2028-06-12); lock Phase 2 design freeze. Within 6 months (by Month 4 = 2027-02-12).

10. Assertions Without Evidence

Does each critical claim (excluding timeline and budget) include at least one verifiable piece of evidence?

Level: 🛑 High

Justification: Rated HIGH because seven critical operational and financial claims lack verifiable artifacts: (1) insurer and fire-authority written approval for pre-treatment hazards (required by Month 6 = 2027-04-12); (2) multi-year binding host-archive agreements (Month 6 = 2027-04-12); (3) binding funder commitments ≥50% Phase 1 (Month 3 = 2027-01-12); (4) parts-depletion model with MTBF and re-manufacture validation (Month 2 = 2026-12-12); (5) AI pre-screening validation on real degraded samples showing precision/recall ≥75% (Month 8 = 2027-06-12); (6) reconciled cost audit locking staffing model (Month 4 = 2027-02-12); (7) written stewardship commitment for perpetual storage post-Month 120 (2036-10-12) (Month 36 = 2029-10-12). All are prerequisite to gate decisions and partnership participation but do not yet exist. Absence of any one blocks Phase 1 or Phase 2 gates.

Mitigation: Designate an owner and acceptance criteria for each of seven artifact categories. Programme Director owns funder commitments (Registry by Month 1 = 2026-11-12, conversions by Month 3 = 2027-01-12). Risk/Legal Lead owns insurer/fire-authority approvals (application by Month 2 = 2026-12-12, written approval by Month 6 = 2027-04-12). Chief Engineer owns parts model (commissioned Month 1 = 2026-11-12, validated Month 4 = 2027-02-12) and AI accuracy (sampling Month 2 = 2026-12-12, measurement Month 8 = 2027-06-12). Finance Lead owns cost audit (commissioned Month 1 = 2026-11-12, locked Month 4 = 2027-02-12). Establish NO-GO escalation per artifact: if insurer approval denied by Month 9 (2027-07-12), detached pod fallback triggers. If AI precision <75% after one retraining cycle, workflow redesign. If <USD 30M Phase 1 committed by Month 3 (2027-01-12), governance re-assessment of scope.

11. Unclear Deliverables

Are the project's final outputs or key milestones poorly defined, lacking specific criteria for completion, making success difficult to measure objectively?

Level: ⚠️ Medium

Justification: Rated MEDIUM because major recoverable outputs (3.6M items, 200+ PB, 30 MIUs, >90% uptime, >95% digitization success, 0 shipping damage) are quantified with measurable gate criteria by phase and site. However, critical non-recoverable deliverables remain abstract: perpetual stewardship of 200+ PB beyond Month 120 (2036-10-12) lacks a named steward, committed funding source, or chosen custody model; AI pre-screening pipeline (claimed 75% precision/recall) is unvalidated on real content; parts-depletion model required Month 2 (2026-12-12) is not yet produced; source agreements and knowledge-base documentation are specified as required but not yet signed or completed. Recovery success is tied to verifiable phase gates; stewardship and infrastructure durability are deferred to future validation without explicit acceptance criteria or ownership.

Mitigation: Chief Engineer and Programme Director: By Month 4 (2027-02-12), publish SMART acceptance criteria for the seven most-abstract deliverables: (1) Perpetual Stewardship: Named archive, signed 20-year commitment letter, funded format-migration mechanism specified. (2) AI Precision/Recall: Measured on 100–200 real degraded samples per category-format-degradation pair, report by Month 8 (2027-06-12). (3) Parts-Depletion Model: MTBF distributions per deck type, cannibalization yield, re-manufacture trigger at 50% depletion, signed-off by retained mentors and independent engineer. (4) Source Agreements: Three signed pilot agreements with tiered indemnity and jurisdiction-specific terms by Month 6 (2027-04-12). (5) Knowledge Base: 50–80 documented competencies per line type in video and written form, successor competency assessments by Month 30 (2029-04-12). (6) Fleet Sunset: One chosen end-state option (transfer, retained core, or rental pool) with successor-body identity and transition plan by Month 36 (2029-10-12). (7) Insurer/Fire Approval: Written approval letters from one pilot site's insurer and fire authority by Month 6 (2027-04-12), replicable to all sites. Each deliverable includes: acceptance criteria, independent verification method, assigned owner, and checkpoint date.

12. Gold Plating

Does the plan add unnecessary features, complexity, or cost beyond the core goal?

Level: 🛑 High

Justification: Rated HIGH because the Restoration Intervention Ceiling decision (Decision 8) mandates retaining wideband head signals and versioned AI restoration layers alongside compressed preservation masters, multiplying storage demand by 3–10× per item. Core project goals: (1) recover 3.6M+ items and 200+ PB within USD 250M cap; (2) sustain >90% uptime and archive partnerships. Wideband retention does NOT directly support either goal—recovery succeeds with lossless compressed derivatives, and uptime depends on equipment availability and parts, not data format choice. The feature supports a secondary aspiration ("post-human value" for future AI reprocessing) and claimed reversibility, but these are NOT stated primary objectives and are NOT binding contractual requirements with archives or funders. Instead, wideband retention multiplies storage 3–10x per item, adding to a perpetual-storage liability of USD 600M–1B over 20 years (estimate) beyond the USD 250M cap, directly conflicting with the budget constraint. Custody, Format, and Access Regime (Decision 7) explicitly acknowledges this trade-off: "keeping raw wideband data multiplies storage and egress demand on a plan already stressed at petabyte scale." The plan defers the decision to Month 6 (2027-04-12) without justification or benefit case.

Mitigation: Chief Engineer and Custody Lead: Commission a one-page Benefit Case Review for wideband retention (by Month 6 = 2027-04-12) specifying: (1) KPI: % of items with recoverable raw captures (target >=80% by Month 120 = 2036-10-12); (2) Owner: Data Stewardship Lead; (3) Estimated cost: ~USD 600M–1B for perpetual wideband storage and format migration over 20 years (estimate); (4) Justification: How does wideband retention support primary goals (cost-per-item below USD 100, >90% uptime, 3.6M items by Month 120 = 2036-10-12)? If benefit case cannot justify the storage multiplier within the USD 250M cap or via new funding source, move wideband retention to Post-Month 120 (2036-10-12) backlog and adopt inline-only restoration (compressed derivatives only) as Phase 1 baseline. If retained, identify committed steward and funding source for perpetual storage by Month 36 (2029-10-12).

13. Staffing Fit & Rationale

Do the roles, capacity, and skills match the work, or is the plan under- or over-staffed?

Level: 🛑 High

Justification: Rated HIGH because the Vintage Equipment Sustainment Engineer is the single point of failure for sustaining >90% uptime using a finite, depleting 300–500 machine stockpile. This expertise in tape-deck azimuth alignment, 3D-printed part fabrication tolerances (±0.05mm), and retired-engineer mentoring is extinct in commercial markets (no demand outside heritage preservation). Globally, ~20–50 individuals hold this competency; aging 70–80 means the hiring window closes within 2–3 years. No substitute vendor or outsourcing path exists.

Mitigation: Recruit and secure written 24-month contract with the Vintage Equipment Sustainment Engineer by Month 1 (2026-11-12), offering USD 80–120K loaded cost plus retention bonus. Commission parts-depletion model and 3D-printing tolerance validation by Month 2 (2026-12-12). Identify and credential 2–3 successor engineers per line type for 18–24 month intensive mentoring by Month 4 (2027-02-12) to mitigate attrition risk.

14. Legal Minefield

Does the plan involve activities with high legal, regulatory, or ethical exposure, such as potential lawsuits, corruption, illegal actions, or societal harm?

Level: ⚠️ Medium

Justification: Rated MEDIUM because the plan acknowledges controlling regimes (fire codes, GDPR, UK DPA, data-residency rules, customs procedures, source-agreement protocols) and assigns clear ownership (Risk/Legal Lead, Privacy Officer, Site Coordinator) with milestone dates (insurer/fire approval Month 6 = 2027-04-12; DPIA and source-agreement templates Month 3 = 2027-01-12; customs pathway Month 4 = 2027-02-12). A credible pathway exists, but actual written approvals, binding stewardship commitments, and operationalized regulatory compliance are unmapped and untested. If fire authority or insurer denies pre-treatment approval at all three pilot sites or permits only detached pods (USD 1.5–4.5M, +4–6 weeks per site), cost and schedule cascade. If GDPR transfer restrictions or data-residency rules force federated or in-country storage not budgeted, perpetual-storage funding gap expands. Lead times are tight and discovery of adverse findings by Month 6 (2027-04-12) risks 4–8 week pilot delays.

Mitigation: Risk and Legal Compliance Lead: By Month 1 (2026-11-12), map all applicable regimes per planned jurisdiction (fire codes, GDPR/DPA, customs, zoning, e-waste, heritage regulations) and assign a Regulatory Approval Matrix (authority, required artifact, lead time, prerequisite). By Month 2 (2026-12-12), engage 3+ fire-safety/insurance specialists and commission a Hazard Control Standard submission package for one representative jurisdiction. By Month 3 (2027-01-12), publish standardized source-agreement template with jurisdiction-specific legal annexes and obtain preliminary feedback from 3 pilot archives. By Month 6 (2027-04-12), obtain written fire-authority and insurer approval at one pilot site and use letter as template for all subsequent sites; sign three pilot host agreements; escalate any approval denial to governance and activate detached-pod fallback design (USD 0.5–1.5M, +4–6 weeks per site, rebaseline timeline).

15. Lacks Operational Sustainability

Even if the project is successfully completed, can it be sustained, maintained, and operated effectively over the long term without ongoing issues?

Level: 🛑 High

Justification: Rated HIGH because operational costs (recomputed ~USD 530M unconstrained vs. USD 250M cap) are unsustainable; funding gap (~USD 280M) is unfunded; Phase 3 budget (USD 70M) cannot sustain 15 units for 60 months without new revenue; post-Month 120 (2036-10-12) perpetual storage (USD 600M–1B estimated) has no committed steward; mentoring window for retiring engineers (ages 70–80) closes by Month 48 (2030-10-12), leaving Phase 3 (Months 60–120 = 2031-10-12 to 2036-10-12) at risk; no end-state or successor-body stewardship is locked.

Mitigation: By Month 3 (2027-01-12), establish Funding Commitment Registry and identify sources to close ~USD 280M gap (host cost-sharing, new funders, or unit-count reduction to ~14). By Month 36 (2029-10-12), secure written stewardship commitment from ≥1 national archive for perpetual storage and identify post-Month 120 (2036-10-12) funding mechanism (endowment, government pledge, or successor-body revenue model). By Month 48 (2030-10-12), complete successor-engineer competency validation and transition plan to successor bodies.

16. Infeasible Constraints

Does the project depend on overcoming constraints that are practically insurmountable, such as obtaining permits that are almost certain to be denied?

Level: ⚠️ Medium

Justification: Rated MEDIUM because hard constraints (fire-authority and insurer approvals for pre-treatment hazards, zoning permits for temporary containers, occupancy and egress codes) are not yet validated at any site, but viable fallback designs exist (detached pre-treatment pod, host-run conservation, deferred processing tier). The plan names required approvals and hazard-control standards as Phase 1 deliverables (Months 2–6 = 2026-12-12 to 2027-04-12) and treats first-site approval as a replicable template for all 30 residencies. Fire-authority and insurer sign-off carry 4–8 week lead times each; approval denial triggers USD 1.5–4.5M fallback cost and +4–18 weeks aggregate delay across three pilots, compressing evidence before Phase 2 gate (Month 24 = 2028-10-12). Calendar risk is material but not existential: detached-pod fallback is designed and priced. Legal/regulatory discovery risk is medium: five or more site rejections (17–25% capacity loss) would force unit count reduction, but this is a remediation scenario, not a blocked path.

Mitigation: Risk and Legal Compliance Lead: By Month 2 (2026-12-12), engage one specialist fire-safety engineer and one insurance broker with cultural-heritage experience; commission a Hazard Control Standard specifying sealed oven design, thermostat tolerance, smoke/fume detection, fire suppression for archival materials, and VOC exhaust filtration per NFPA standards. By Month 4 (2027-02-12), submit technical drawings, MSDS data for consumables, and emergency-response plan to one representative fire authority and insurer; request written conditional approval or explicit denial with required modifications by Month 6 (2027-04-12). If approval is granted, use approval letter as template for all subsequent sites and budget USD 50–100K for jurisdiction-specific permit adaptation per region. If approval is denied or conditional on detached pod, activate fallback: design separate 20-ft pre-treatment container (USD 0.5–1.5M each, +4–6 weeks setup); obtain fire-authority approval for detached design by Month 8 (2027-06-12); rebaseline pilot schedule and Phase 1 contingency. Define NO-GO threshold: if fire-authority and insurer approval cannot be obtained at any of three pilot sites by Month 9 (2027-07-12), escalate to governance and consider vendor-operated or deferred-risk model.

17. External Dependencies

Does the project depend on critical external factors, third parties, suppliers, or vendors that may fail, delay, or be unavailable when needed?

Level: 🛑 High

Justification: Rated HIGH because external dependencies carrying single points of failure with no tested failover exist across three critical domains: (1) Vintage equipment sustainment: 300–500 decommissioned decks and scanners are a finite, globally-scattered stock with no identified alternate supplier; once acquired, they are consumed by 30 units' continuous operation and cannot be replenished at same-economy scale. No secondary stockpile or vendor is named. (2) Retired-engineer expertise: 6–8 broadcast engineers (aged 70–80) hold irreplaceable knowledge of tape-deck azimuth alignment, 3D-printed part tolerances, and head calibration. No backup pool exists; attrition before Month 48 (2030-10-12) leaves Phase 3 (Months 60–120 = 2031-10-12 to 2036-10-12) without diagnostic capacity. (3) Archive partnerships: On-site residencies depend entirely on insurer and fire-authority approval of pre-treatment hazards (ovens, generators, media storage). One handling incident or privacy breach could cascade partnership termination across the network. No fallback archive path or alternative deployment model is pre-negotiated. (4) Perpetual data stewardship: 200+ PB of recovered masters have no committed steward and no funded post-Month 120 (2036-10-12) storage mechanism; masters become inaccessible if archives demand guarantees they cannot receive. All four dependencies lack tested failover plans.

Mitigation: Risk and Procurement Lead: By Month 2 (2026-12-12), commission a Vendor Redundancy and Fallback Strategy addressing each dependency. (1) Vintage Equipment Failover: Map secondary suppliers of decommissioned broadcast and film equipment in North America, Europe and Japan; negotiate non-binding letters of intent (LOIs) from ≥2 major suppliers committing to supply ≥100 units by Month 4 (2027-02-12) at average cost ≤USD 4K per unit if primary sources become constrained; budget USD 500K–1M for expedited procurement and dual-source procurement for critical line-specific subsystems (tape transports, film scanner optical blocks). (2) Retired-Engineer Mentoring Failover: Secure ≥6–8 mentor contracts (min 2 per line type: Tape, Film, Card) by Month 1 (2026-11-12) with explicit redundancy and cross-training overlap; engage ≥2 successor engineers per mentor and complete competency sign-offs by Month 30 (2029-04-12); document all 50–80 critical repair competencies in permanent video and written protocols accessible to all engineers by Month 4 (2027-02-12). (3) Archive Partnership Failover: By Month 9 (2027-07-12), establish a Priority Waitlist of ≥10 backup archive sites (with pre-assessed readiness and regulatory approval status) ready to receive a unit on 4–6 weeks notice; obtain tiered-indemnity pooled loss reserve (USD 2–5M) from Phase 1 budget to cover unique-item losses if incident occurs; develop Detached Pre-Treatment Pod design (separate 20-ft container, ≥50 meters from archive building) as fallback if on-site pre-treatment approval is denied (USD 0.5–1.5M per pod, +4–6 weeks setup per site). (4) Data Stewardship Failover: By Month 36 (2029-10-12), secure written 20-year stewardship commitment from ≥1 national or regional archive (e.g., Library of Congress, British Library, national archives of Canada/Australia); specify perpetual storage location, two verified geographically-separate copies per master, annual format-migration funding mechanism (perpetual-storage liability estimated at USD 600M–1B over 20 years (estimate) for 200+ PB), and governance structure beyond Month 120 (2036-10-12). If primary steward withdraws, activate secondary steward from ≥2 named backup institutions. Publish Resilience and Continuity Plan by Month 24 (2028-10-12) documenting all failover procedures, thresholds, and activation triggers.

18. Stakeholder Misalignment

Are there conflicting interests, misaligned incentives, or lack of genuine commitment from key stakeholders that could derail the project?

Level: ✅ Low

Justification: Checklist item 18 cannot be answered because the input documents do not define explicit stakeholder incentive structures or conflicting performance goals between two distinct groups. Stakeholder roles and organizations are named (funders, archives, engineers) but their underlying incentives and success metrics are not articulated. Without a stated basis for the analysis, a conflict identification would be invented rather than derived from the plan.

Mitigation: Provide or clarify stakeholder incentive structures in input documents before checklist item 18 is answered. Specify which two stakeholder groups should be analyzed (e.g., "Funder Consortium vs. Host Archives," "Programme Director vs. Retired-Engineer Mentors," or "Technology-Sector Funder vs. Rights Holders") and document their stated goals, success metrics, and performance incentives.

19. No Adaptive Framework

Does the plan lack a clear process for monitoring progress and managing changes, treating the initial plan as final?

Level: 🛑 High

Justification: Rated HIGH because the plan lacks a documented feedback loop, governance review cadence, key performance indicator (KPI) dashboard, change-control process, and explicit thresholds defining when to re-plan or halt the program. The plan names success metrics (>95% digitization success, >80% reconstruction accuracy, >90% uptime, <20% review, zero incidents) and phase gates (Month 24 = 2028-10-12, Month 60 = 2031-10-12, Month 120 = 2036-10-12) but does not specify: (1) monthly variance-tracking mechanism or escalation authority; (2) KPI dashboard ownership and update frequency; (3) who owns and chairs monthly review meetings; (4) decision thresholds (e.g., uptime drops below 90% for 2 consecutive months -> governance escalation); (5) change-control board authority to pause, rework, or halt phase releases. The plan states "publish quarterly Cost-Tracking and Variance Reporting" and "monthly reporting dashboard" as proposals, not as locked governance artifacts. Two critical governance gaps remain unresolved by Month 4 (2027-02-12): (a) no written Monthly Review Charter specifying KPI targets, review cadence, owner accountability, and variance escalation paths; (b) no Governance Decision-Rights Framework specifying which decisions require full Programme Board consensus, which are delegated to committees, and what triggers override or rework. Without these artifacts, monthly program reviews will lack clarity, variance signals may be missed, and Phase 2 and Phase 3 releases will lack a credible quantitative basis.

Mitigation: Finance Lead and Programme Director: By Month 3 (2027-01-12), establish a Monthly Review Charter specifying: (1) KPI Dashboard (uptime % trailing 6 months, cumulative items recovered, cumulative PB, AI flagging rate, review hours per content hour, parts consumption vs. 50% trigger, cost variance %, incident count) updated monthly by end of business day 5 of each month; (2) Monthly Governance Review meeting (first Monday after month-end, 90 minutes, Programme Board plus functional leads) with published agenda and decision log; (3) Variance Escalation Rules: uptime <90% for 2 consecutive months -> root-cause investigation + corrective action plan within 2 weeks or governance pause decision; cumulative cost variance >10% -> finance audit and Phase 2/3 scope re-assessment; any reportable incident (privacy, handling, equipment failure) -> 24-hour escalation + 10-day forensic review + public incident log update. (4) Change-Control Board (3-5 members: Programme Director, Finance Lead, Chief Engineer, Legal Lead, Host Liaison) meets monthly to review proposed design changes, parts substitutions, crew adjustments, and scope modifications; gate design changes behind independent technical review (Month 20 = 2028-06-12 design freeze approval). Owner: Programme Director (review charter), Finance Lead (KPI dashboard), Change-Control Board Secretary (meeting coordination). Deliverable: Signed Monthly Review Charter and Change-Control Procedures document. Date: Within 3 months (Month 3 = 2027-01-12).

20. Uncategorized Red Flags

Are there any other significant risks or major issues that are not covered by other items in this checklist but still threaten the project's viability?

Level: 🛑 High

Justification: Rated HIGH because three critical HIGH risks are strongly coupled and share common single points of failure: (1) Staffing-Budget-AI Accuracy coupling: If AI flagging exceeds 25% (unvalidated), reviewer headcount rises about 1.75–2x (roughly USD 14–32M annual payroll overspend, estimate); if mentors (ages 70-80) become unavailable before Month 18 (2028-04-12), successor engineers lack expertise to diagnose failures, driving uptime below 90% and cascading crew burnout and budget collapse. (2) Parts-Mentor-Uptime coupling: Finite 300-500 machine stockpile is consumed by continuous operation; if MTBF is shorter than modeled or 3D-printed parts miss tolerance specs, spares exhaust mid-programme; if mentors exit before Month 18 (2028-04-12), engineers cannot validate replacements, forcing emergency USD 15-25M stockpile refresh unbudgeted and Phase 3 unit reduction. (3) Trust-Privacy-Stewardship coupling: If AI false-negatives permit PII upload or any handling incident destroys a unique collection, insurer cancellation cascades partnership termination (2-5 sites, 10-17% capacity loss); if no stewardship commitment for 200+ PB post-Month 120 (2036-10-12), remaining archives demand perpetual-storage guarantees before releasing originals, forcing 3-5 additional site deferrals and network shrinkage from 30 to ~20 units. Overlooked critical cascading risk: Funder Commitment Cliff at Phase 2 Gate (Month 24 = 2028-10-12)—if gate evidence reveals unmet thresholds (flagging >25%, precision/recall <75%, cost variance >10%), Phase 2 release is held 6-12 months for rework or redesign (2-4 week retraining or 6-9 month design cycle). Funder re-engagement and committee re-approval across 15+ organizations compresses Phase 2 from 36 months to 24-30 months, reducing residencies from 12 to 8-10 sites (150K-300K items deferred); Phase 3 start slips to Month 66-72 (2032-04-12 to 2032-10-12) and final unit count drops to 10-15 instead of 15. Media degradation (10-30 year lifespan) continues unrecovered; 3.6M-item target becomes ~2.7M-3.2M, breaking the core mission.

Mitigation: Risk Owner (Programme Director) and Chief Engineer: Establish Interdependency Risk Map and Cascade-Failure Protocol by Month 2 (2026-12-12). (1) Coupled-Risk Dashboard: Track AI flagging rate, mentor contract status, parts inventory level, cumulative cost variance, uptime % and partnership incidents on a single monthly dashboard; define automated escalation if any metric drifts toward threshold (flagging >22%, mentors <6, variance >8%, uptime <92%, incident logged). (2) NO-GO Thresholds and Governance Triggers: If (a) AI precision/recall <70% after retraining (governance re-assessment), OR (b) flagging >30% (redesign review workflow), OR (c) mentors <6 by Month 1 (2026-11-12), OR (d) parts depletion model shows spares exhausted before Month 60 (2031-10-12), OR (e) cumulative variance >10% at any gate, OR (f) any reportable incident occurs → immediately escalate to Programme Board and activate corresponding contingency playbook (design rework, crew reduction, unit-count reduction, or partnership stabilization). (3) Phase 2 Gate Pre-Assessment (Month 20 = 2028-06-12): 4 weeks before Phase 2 gate decision, forecast which thresholds will be missed and pre-brief funders on contingency scenarios (full release, conditional release with rework, or Phase 2 deferral); confirm funder appetite for each scenario before evidence is complete, reducing post-gate committee cycles to 2-4 weeks instead of 6-12 weeks. (4) Multi-Scenario Phase 2-3 Schedule (Month 22 = 2028-08-12): Publish three master schedules (baseline: Phase 2 start Month 24, 12 = 2028-10-12, 2027-10-12 sites, 15 units by Month 120 = 2036-10-12; rework: Phase 2 start Month 28-32 = 2029-02-12 to 2029-06-12, 10 sites, 12 units; reduction: Phase 2 start Month 24, 8 = 2028-10-12, 2027-06-12 sites, 10 units final) and pre-negotiate funder and archive acceptance of each scenario to eliminate post-gate re-baselining delay. (5) Contingency Activation Playbooks: Pre-develop playbooks for each coupled-failure scenario: (a) AI+Crew: if flagging >25%, activate Tiered Review Redesign (delegate low-risk to archive, high-risk to experts, escalate disputes) and recalibrate crew from 12-15 to 20-25 per unit within 2 weeks; (b) Mentor+Parts: if <6 mentors committed, immediately contract 2-3 external broadcast consultants and accelerate successor competency sign-off to Month 24 (2028-10-12); (c) Trust+Stewardship: if any incident occurs, activate Archive Stabilization Protocol (24-hour insurer notification, 48-hour incident log publication, public commitment to stewardship letter from named archive by Month 28 = 2029-02-12); (d) Funder Cliff: if Phase 2 gate evidence variance >10%, activate Funder Pre-Brief and Scenario Selection 4 weeks before gate decision (avoid post-gate delays). (6) Stop Rule: If two or more coupled risks hit their NO-GO thresholds simultaneously (e.g., AI precision <75% AND mentors <6 AND cost variance >10%), halt all Phase 2 procurement and conduct 60-day governance re-assessment; do not release Phase 2 tranche until re-baseline is approved. Deliverable: Interdependency Risk Map (cross-impact matrix showing which risks trigger which cascades, with conditional probabilities), Coupled-Risk Dashboard template, three Phase 2-3 Master Schedules, and five Contingency Activation Playbooks (one per scenario). Owner: Programme Director (governance), Chief Engineer (technical cascades), Finance Lead (cost variance). Date: Month 2 (2026-12-12) map and dashboard; Month 20 (2028-06-12) Phase 2 pre-assessment; Month 22 (2028-08-12) three-scenario schedule publication and funder pre-brief.

Contradictions between the core documents, after repair.

Consistency: first pass found 3 high / 6 medium / 1 low contradictions. Repair: round 1: 51 edits → 0 high / 9 medium. Shown below: the final check of the repaired documents (0 high / 9 medium / 0 low).

1. Headline scope stated within the cap vs what the cap can fund (🔴 High) — needs a project decision

  • Project plan goal statement; executive summary Purpose and Goals; pitch overview: Goal: build 30 MIUs and deliver 3.6M+ items and 200+ PB "within the USD 250M cap".
  • Project plan Achievable; review plan Review 1; self-audit items 3, 7; premortem FM1: Cap supports ~47% of scope (~14 unit-equivalents, ~1.7M items, ~95 PB); uncapped cost ~USD 530M; unfunded gap ~USD 280M with no committed source. NO-GO triggers (only ~14 units fundable; fewer than 24 units) are already met on these numbers.
  • Why it conflicts: The target is framed as achievable inside the cap while the same documents show it is about half-funded and that the stated stop conditions are already tripped. Phase 3 capex financing for the 15 final MIUs is also unassigned.
  • Suggested resolution: State the funded scope (~14 unit-equivalents) as the baseline commitment and show 30 units / 3.6M items as conditional on closing the gap. The decision options are: (a) host or consortium cash cost-share per MIU, (b) new government or consortium funders, (c) rights-holder-approved technology-sector funding, (d) reduced unit count or crew size. The project decision is who finances Phase 2-3 MIU capex (USD 105M at midpoint) and whether the Month 4 lock proceeds at reduced scope.

Site-loss figures also imply ~120K items per residency against 6-12 month residencies of ~8-24K items.
